subtype: Approach: puts a stuck problem aside overnight and returns fresh [Thinking]
passage: Aadhya here, writing down what I saw of my flatmate Vivek's app project this week. Until dinner on Tuesday, Vivek kept rearranging the booking screens: six tabs, then a side menu, then tabs again, muttering that every layout hid something important. Around nine he closed the laptop and said, "I'm done, I can't see it." He watched a cricket highlights video and went to bed. At breakfast he was already sketching on a napkin. "One screen," he said. "The list on top and the button fixed at the bottom. I was trying to make it hold everything. It didn't need to." I can't know what went on in his head overnight, but the fix took him ten minutes. He says sleep did the sorting.

qa.q: What did Vivek do after closing the laptop at nine?
qa.a: Vivek watched a cricket highlights video and went to bed.

qa.q: What was Vivek feeling when he said "I can't see it"?
qa.a: Vivek felt stuck and worn out with the layout, after rearranging the screens again and again.

qa.q: What could Vivek do if he was still stuck after a night's rest?
qa.a: Vivek could show the layout to a classmate or try it with a couple of users, since a fresh view or new information gives more to work with than more waiting.

qa.q: Why is Aadhya careful about saying what happened in Vivek's head overnight?
qa.a: Aadhya only saw what Vivek did and said, so cannot know for sure what went on in Vivek's mind.

grounding: Shows a student leaving a stuck design decision overnight and seeing a simpler layout next morning.

subtype: Approach: uses waiting as a way to avoid a needed decision [Pitfall]
passage:
In the Class 12 counselling room, Aparna slid the two course forms across the desk. "The last date is the fifteenth. Have you picked?"

Santosh shrugged. "I'll sleep on it."

A week later he said it again, and the week after that. Each time Aparna asked what he had found out, he said, "Nothing new, I'm still thinking." He had not opened either college website or asked a senior about the hostel. On the sixteenth he came in with the forms still unsigned and read the notice on the board.

"It closed yesterday." He stared at the paper. "I thought more time would just make it clear."

Aparna pulled a chair up beside him and asked what he wanted to do about it now.

qa.q: On which date had the forms closed?
qa.a: The forms closed on the fifteenth, the day before Santosh read the notice.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling as he read the notice on the board?
qa.a: Santosh was shocked and probably regretful, staring at the paper after hoping that more time would make things clear.

qa.q: What could Santosh have done with those weeks instead of only waiting?
qa.a: Santosh could have set a date to decide, opened the college websites and asked a senior about the hostel, so there were new facts to think about.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt each time Santosh said he would sleep on it?
qa.a: Aparna may have felt concerned and a little helpless, seeing nothing new gathered while the last date came closer.

grounding: Shows a student using 'sleeping on it' with no end date and gathering nothing, so a deadline passes.

subtype: Approach: sleeps on a big offer after gathering the facts [Thinking]
passage:
'They want an answer by Friday,' Jatin said, setting his phone on the pantry table. Reena raised her eyebrows. 'And?'

'A bigger title, a longer commute, a team I have met twice.' He pulled a sticky pad from his pocket and drew two columns. Salary went up, and so did travel time. Learning looked better; the manager's style was unknown. 'I'm so excited I could say yes right now,' he said. 'That's exactly why I won't. If it still looks good tomorrow when I'm calm, it's real.'

Reena stirred her tea. 'Anything you still want to ask them?'

'Yes, what the first three months look like. I'll call at ten.'

He slid the note into his wallet and went back to his desk.

qa.q: What did Jatin draw on the sticky pad?
qa.a: Jatin drew two columns, with salary and learning on one side and longer travel and an unknown manager's style on the other.

qa.q: How was Jatin feeling about the offer, and why did that make him wait?
qa.a: Jatin was excited, and he did not want excitement to decide on its own, so he wanted a calm look the next day.

qa.q: What could Jatin do if he still felt unsure the next day?
qa.a: Jatin could ask for more information, such as what the first three months look like, or talk with someone who works with that team.

qa.q: How might Reena see Jatin's choice to wait?
qa.a: Reena might find it sensible, since Reena nodded, offered another question to ask and did not push for a quick answer.

grounding: Shows a professional listing pros and cons and then waiting one night so excitement does not decide alone.

subtype: Approach: sets a decision time and a small question to reflect on [Revision]
passage: Farhan, come and sit. You asked how I stop dithering; well, Parveen was the worst of all once. Let me tell you about the Pune offer. I was twenty-five, and for five days I told my manager, "Let me think." On the fifth evening I heard myself say it again and laughed, because I was not thinking at all, only putting it off. So I tore a sticky note and wrote: answer by Thursday, noon. Under it I wrote one question: which choice would I hate not having tried? I stuck it on my mirror and slept on it. By Thursday morning I knew, and at eleven I told my manager yes. The fear had not gone. But the date and the question gave my thinking somewhere to land.

qa.q: What question did Parveen write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Parveen wrote one question: which choice would I hate not having tried.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel on the fifth evening when saying "Let me think" again?
qa.a: Parveen felt amused and a little caught out, realising it was putting off rather than thinking.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Parveen's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Parveen wrote a fixed time, Thursday noon, and one question, which turned open-ended waiting into a night of thinking with a clear focus.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen those five days of "Let me think"?
qa.a: The manager may have felt uncertain and unable to plan, and perhaps worried that the offer would be turned down.

grounding: Shows a person who notices repeated postponing and sets an answer time plus one question to think about overnight.

subtype: Approach: gives a task a fixed time slot [Action]
passage:
The house was full of relatives for the wedding, and someone was tuning a dholak downstairs. Abhinav had maths homework and wanted to go out to play later. His sister Nandini handed him the kitchen timer.

"Twenty minutes," he said, turning the dial, and he sat in a corner of the balcony with his notebook. He did the first six sums, put a star beside a hard one, and the timer rang while he was halfway through the seventh. He stopped, even though he wanted to finish. He drank water, stretched, and looked at the street for five minutes. Then he opened his science book and set the timer again.

qa.q: What did Nandini hand to Abhinav?
qa.a: Nandini handed him the kitchen timer.

qa.q: What did Abhinav feel when the timer rang halfway through the seventh sum?
qa.a: Abhinav was probably torn, since he wanted to finish the seventh sum but stopped anyway when the timer rang.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do about the hard sum he starred?
qa.a: Abhinav could ask Nandini or the teacher about it, or try it again after the break, so it does not eat up the rest of his time.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Abhinav's plan in such a noisy house?
qa.a: Nandini might be glad the timer helped him stay focused despite the noise, and relieved he was doing the homework instead of skipping it.

grounding: Shows a boy giving maths homework a fixed twenty-minute slot, stopping at the ring and taking a short break.

subtype: Approach: fills a weekly timetable with slots for subjects [Action]
passage: The power cut at six meant no fan, and the room Lavanya shared with her younger brother Anirban was hot and loud. Board exams were five months away, and Lavanya was tired of that feeling of not knowing what to study next. With a ruler and a marker she drew a chart on the back of an old calendar: seven to seven-forty, maths; then a short break; then science, another break, then social studies. She taped it to the wall above the study table. When the lights came back she started the first block. Anirban read the chart and asked, "Where's my slot?" Lavanya laughed and wrote his drawing time in blue, beside hers.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya tape the chart?
qa.a: Lavanya taped it to the wall above the study table.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling before she drew the chart?
qa.a: Lavanya was tired of not knowing what to study next, and probably anxious about the board exams five months away.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do if one subject keeps needing more than its block?
qa.a: Lavanya could lengthen that block on the chart after noticing it, or add a second block for it on another day, so the plan fits what really happens.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt about the chart?
qa.a: Anirban may have felt left out at first, as his question shows, and then included once his drawing time went up beside hers.

grounding: Shows a Class 10 student filling her evening with timed subject slots and breaks and marking them on a wall chart.

subtype: Approach: caps a task at a set time to fight perfectionism [Thinking]
passage:
Thursday, 10:40 pm. The whole draft is done, which I did not think would happen today. Usually I rewrite my first paragraph nine times and never see page two. This morning I told myself: introduction gets one hour, that's it, even if it's ugly. A draft that exists beats a perfect paragraph, and I can polish later. I put the phone timer next to the laptop. At forty minutes I hated my second sentence but left it. When the alarm went I stopped mid-thought, typed "fix opening line later" in brackets, and started the methods section. The middle went easily once I quit polishing. Sahil asked at dinner if I was okay, because I was smiling at a spreadsheet. Tomorrow I read it all again. Tonight, it exists.

Ojas

qa.q: How long did Ojas allow for the introduction?
qa.a: Ojas said the introduction gets one hour.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling while smiling at a spreadsheet?
qa.a: Ojas felt relieved and pleased at having got the whole draft done in one day.

qa.q: What could Ojas do if one hour is still not enough for a hard section?
qa.a: Ojas could set a second short box after a break, or mark the rough parts and come back, so the draft still keeps moving.

qa.q: How might Sahil have seen Ojas's mood at dinner?
qa.a: Sahil may have been surprised and a bit amused, since smiling at a spreadsheet is unusual.

grounding: Shows a student capping the introduction at one hour to fight perfectionism, moving on and finishing the draft.

subtype: Approach: packs the schedule so tightly that one overrun ruins the day [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Pradeep coloured every hour of Wednesday in his calendar, nine to six, with no gap between blocks, not even for tea. He showed Rukmini at the next desk. "Fully planned," he said, and grinned.

Wednesday. The client call meant to end at ten went on till eleven-fifteen. The report block was gone, the email block was gone, and by noon every box after it sat in the wrong place. He looked at the red pile and closed the calendar. The afternoon became replies and coffee refills, and the report was not sent.

Friday. Rukmini stopped at his desk. "I waited for the report until Thursday evening." Pradeep opened the calendar to the empty Wednesday. "It was all planned," he said.

qa.q: Until what time did the client call run?
qa.a: The client call went on till eleven-fifteen.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he showed Rukmini his calendar?
qa.a: Pradeep was proud and pleased, since he grinned and said it was fully planned.

qa.q: What could Pradeep change so that one long call does not wreck the day?
qa.a: Pradeep could leave short gaps between blocks and keep one flexible slot for overruns, so a long call only nudges things instead of breaking them.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have been affected by the missed report?
qa.a: Rukmini waited until Thursday evening, so may have been frustrated or worried about follow-on work, without knowing what had gone wrong.

grounding: Shows an employee boxing every hour with no slack so that one overrunning call makes him drop the schedule and miss a report.

subtype: Approach: adjusts box lengths from tracked actuals and adds gaps [Revision]
passage: Joseph here. Tenzin, who sits opposite me, keeps a small notebook by her keyboard, and for two weeks I watched her write down start and end times for everything. I asked once. "My boxes are wrong," she said, "but I need the numbers first." On the second Friday she opened her schedule and changed it. The weekly report block went from one hour to ninety minutes, because her notes showed it never took less. After every meeting she put a fifteen-minute gap labelled "notes and messages", since she had been rushing into the next task with half-written follow-ups. Her week looked calmer after that, though I cannot say what she felt, only that she stopped skipping lunch. She told me the first week with the new boxes ended with everything sent on time.

qa.q: What did Tenzin change the report block to?
qa.a: The weekly report block went from one hour to ninety minutes.

qa.q: What did Tenzin want from writing down the times?
qa.a: Tenzin wanted the real numbers before changing anything, expecting the notes to show how the boxes should change.

qa.q: What else could Tenzin do if meetings still overrun the gap?
qa.a: Tenzin could keep tracking for another week and lengthen the gap, or ask for shorter meetings, using the notes as evidence.

qa.q: Why does Joseph say only what Tenzin did and not how Tenzin felt?
qa.a: Joseph only watched from the opposite desk and cannot know Tenzin's feelings for sure; the notebook, the schedule and the lunches are what could be seen.

grounding: Shows a person noting real task durations for two weeks and then lengthening the report block and adding gaps after meetings.

subtype: Approach: ticks off items on a list before leaving [Action]
passage:
Every morning before the bus, Selin stood at the front door of the third-floor flat with a pencil tied to a string. Taped to the door was her list: books, lunch box, water bottle, homework. Her mother Sofia was still tying her hair at the mirror.

"Books," Selin said, tapping the bag before she drew a tick. "Lunch box." It was on the kitchen table, so she ran back for it. "Water bottle." She unzipped the side pocket and looked inside. "Homework." She pulled the maths sheet halfway out, saw her name on top, pushed it back and ticked.

Four ticks. "Ready!" she called, and Sofia gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: What four things were on Selin's list?
qa.a: Selin's list said books, lunch box, water bottle and homework.

qa.q: How was Selin feeling as she called "Ready!"?
qa.a: Selin felt pleased and confident because every item on the list had a tick.

qa.q: What could Selin do if she forgets to use the list on a rushed morning?
qa.a: Selin could pack her bag the evening before and use the list to check it again at the door, or ask Sofia for a reminder.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel about the list on the door?
qa.a: Sofia might feel relieved that Selin can check the bag alone, so that mornings are less rushed.

grounding: Shows a girl ticking each item on a door checklist before leaving for school.
